Manual

Everything the FM-1 does under Tonitor. New here? Start with Playing it; to install, see Install.

Not a groovebox

No tempo, no steps, no patterns, no drum kit.

Tonitor is for sound heard for itself: texture, grain, movement and slow transformation. You play drones, gestures and textures, layer them, loop them freely out of time with one another, and shape them while they play. It suits acousmatic and electroacoustic work as much as live ambient music, dark ambient above all.

Playing it Generative paths Macros Envelope BALLSY Latched keys Chords Direction and speed Copying a track The loopers The screen Scales Presets Sessions The granulator The distortion The delay The reverb The engines FM — six operators, DX7 style ANIMA — a lo-fi synthesizer played by a simulated hand CALIGULA — an organism RUSSOLO — noise, logic and broken buffers DRUID — strings and resonant bodies BAYAREA — a West Coast voice

Playing it

ControlWhat it does
FX SEL ENV LFO EDIT GLO (top row)choose track 1 2 3 4 5 6. The chosen track's button is lit; the others glow while they sound. Held (0.8 s): copy the track, or paste the copy onto it — see Copying a track.
PRESETS knobthe chosen track's engine: FM, ANIMA, CALIGULA, RUSSOLO, DRUID or BAYAREA, left to right. Each track keeps a sound of each engine, so turning back finds the sound it had.
HOMEa new sound for the chosen track, on its engine (never the same family twice in a row). HOME lights for a moment.
SHIFT + HOMEa new sound of the same family (kind, species) as the chosen track's sound — to explore a family you like. The screen says SAME FAMILY.
OCT− / OCT+the chosen track's octave, −3 to +3. OCT− is lit below the middle, OCT+ above.
SHIFT + OCT− / OCT+every loop of every track down or up one step of the scale (see the loopers).
SHIFT + a track's button held + OCT− / OCT+that track's loops only, down or up one step of the scale (TRANSP T3 +2).
the white keysplay the chosen track in the scale chosen (ARP): the first white key is the root, each white key the next note of the scale, up across all 16. Voices come from one pool of twelve shared by all the tracks: a note takes a free voice, so a track has as many as its notes need — a chord on one, a single line on another — and a new note never cuts the release of the one before it while voices are free. With the twelve all busy, a new note takes the release that has rung longest (on any track), else the oldest note held on its own track, else the oldest held anywhere. (CALIGULA and RUSSOLO are one organism a track, outside the pool.) A key lifted ends its note on the track it was played on, so a held note keeps sounding while you choose and play another track. The keys you hold on the chosen track light up.
the rightmost black keySHIFT (lit while held). Hold white keys and press SHIFT: they latch — they keep sounding after you let go, and their keys stay lit. Hold SHIFT and press a lit key to let go of it.
the two leftmost black keysthe chosen track's generative path: the first AMBIENT, the second EXPERIMENTAL (lit while chosen; the screen says which). Pressing the lit one again goes back to OPEN. See below.
the 3rd black key from the rightthe ENVELOPE page, up and down (lit while up): KNOB 1–4 set the chosen track's attack, decay, sustain and release. With SHIFT: the sound's own envelope again. See Envelope.
the black key before SHIFTEDIT, on and off (lit while on): KNOB 1–4 become four macros that shape the chosen track's sound. See Macros. With SHIFT: the chosen track's physics sequencer, BALLSY, on and off (EDIT blinks while it runs); held (0.6 s) while it runs, its page up or down. A short press is always EDIT. See BALLSY.
the 3rd black keychord mode for the chosen track: held (0.6 s), on or off — CHO at the top left of the screen while on, the key lit; pressed, the next chord form (its name on the screen). See Chords.
the 4th, 5th and 6th black keysthe chosen track's loops REVERSE (played backwards), PENDULUM (forwards and backwards in turn) or RANDOM (the notes in an order drawn at random); pressed again, forwards. Lit while on. See Direction and speed.
the 7th and 8th black keysthe chosen track's loops at HALF SPEED or DOUBLE SPEED; pressed again, normal speed. Lit while on.
all black keysplay no notes. They glow dimly while off and are fully lit while on — the loop direction and speed keys only while the chosen track's loops play; SHIFT is lit only while held.
ARPthe SCALE page (ARP lit): SELECT chooses the root (C to B), ALGORITHM the scale. The root is shown very large, the scale under it; what you just turned flashes black on white. ARP again, or a track button, goes back.
RECthe chosen track's looper. Press to arm a new loop (REC flashes, the band shows ARMED and its number); the first note you play starts it (REC lights; REC and the number). Press REC again to end it: the loop is exactly as long as from that first note to this press, and it starts playing at once, round and round. Press REC again while it plays to overdub: the same again, a new loop over the others — up to 10 loops a track.
SHIFT + RECthe chosen track's loops VARY, on and off (VAR at the top right of the screen while on): each note they play gets a random level (from −10 dB to full) and a random length (50 ms to 1.5 s) instead of the recorded one, and now and then, at odds of its own, it is changed or joined: dropped this time round (5 %), late by 5–40 ms (25 %), an octave up or down (8 %), replaced or joined by a note that was not recorded — a step or two of the scale away, or a fifth (8 %), preceded by a grace note a step away (4 %), struck 2–4 times quickly (4 %), joined by a third or fifth above (10 %), echoed 1–4 times 120–400 ms apart, each quieter, sometimes climbing or falling a step each time (15 %); the notes of a chord are sometimes strummed 20–60 ms apart (12 %). Every note stays in the scale. Applies to all its overdubs. Stored in sessions; ends when the track's loops are emptied.
REC held (1 s)empty the chosen track's looper, all its loops: the whole screen flashes LOOP n / EMPTY.
PLAYpressed and let go: stop the chosen track's loops, or play them again, each from its start. Held: the chosen track's loops on the white keys, to bring each in or take it out (see The loopers). PLAY is lit while they play. SHIFT and PLAY, from any track: if any loop plays, every loop on every track stops (LOOPS OFF; the loops are kept); if none plays, every loop there is starts, all together from their starts (LOOPS ON). PLAY alone still starts or stops the chosen track's own.
SELECT knobthe chosen track's level: 1.5 dB a click, from OFF up to +4.5 dB. The message band says it as the knob's share of its turn, OFF and 4 % to 100 % (VOL 74 %); a track starts at 87 % (0 dB).
KNOB 1the chosen track's DJ filter: from the middle (off), left is a resonant low-pass coming down from 20 kHz to ~35 Hz, right a resonant high-pass going up from 16 Hz to ~12 kHz; the further from the middle, the more resonant. While you turn it, and for a second after, the whole screen is its dial (in the track's colour, the mode and cutoff under it: LP 1.2 KHZ). Saved with the session.
KNOB 2the chosen track's granulator: the middle is off (as it starts). Left towards dark ambient: long, overlapping, slowly drifting grains, pitched down now and then, darkened, fed back on themselves, sometimes frozen. Right towards scattering: short, fast grains, their timing, place, pitch and level jittered more and more, reversed, stuttered, full of holes, decimated at the far end. The further from the middle, the more grains and the less of the track. While you turn it, the whole screen is its dial (DARK 40, SCATTER 25, OFF). Saved with the session.
KNOB 3the chosen track's crush: the middle is off (as it starts). Left takes the bit depth down from 16 to 1.5 bits (the sound coarsens, then breaks up, quiet tails gating out); right takes the sample rate down from 44.1 kHz to ~300 Hz (metallic aliasing, then a stepped buzz). Both along curves that keep the first half of the way playable; the rate glides, it does not jump. While you turn it, the whole screen is its dial (BITS 6.5, RATE 2.6K). After the granulator, before the track's limiter. Saved with the session.
KNOB 4the chosen track's reverb send, 0–100 (40 at the start). While you turn it, the whole screen is its dial (SEND 40), as for the filter and the granulator.
SAVEthe SESSIONS page: PRESETS turns through the 64 slots (the number shown very large: red when the slot holds a session, faint grey with EMPTY under it when it does not; the session loaded says LOADED). SAVE on a saved slot loads it; on an empty slot it starts a new session there: a clean slate, as when the FM-1 is switched on — the loops and latches gone, every track on its first engine with new sounds and its settings at their defaults, the scale, reverb and transposition too (the session you were in stays saved as it was) — and the next save goes there. Either way back to playing. A track button goes back without either.
SHIFT + SAVEthe chosen track's engine's PRESETS page (see Presets); SHIFT + SAVE again, or a track button, goes back.
SAVE held (0.8 s)save into the session loaded or chosen, at once; the whole screen flashes SAVED and the number. With none loaded or chosen yet (just after switching on), the first empty slot is offered: PRESETS chooses NO / YES, SAVE answers. On the SESSIONS page, SAVE held saves into the slot shown, whatever is loaded: an empty one asks SAVE NEW; one holding a session asks OVERWRITE? in red, on NO until PRESETS turns it to YES; SAVE answers.
SEQthe REVERB page (SEQ lit). There KNOB 1–4 are SIZE, DECAY, DAMP, MIX. SEQ again, or a track button, goes back.
SHIFT + SEQthe DELAY page (SEQ lit). There KNOB 1–4 are TIME (20 ms – 2 s), FEEDBACK, DAMP, MIX. SHIFT + SEQ again, SEQ (to the REVERB page) or a track button goes back. See The delay.
SHIFT + KNOB 3the chosen track's distortion, 0–100 (0, off, at the start); its dial reads DISTORTION n and the amount. See The distortion.
SHIFT + KNOB 4the chosen track's delay send, 0–100 (0 at the start); its dial reads DELAY n / SEND.
ALGORITHM knobthe chosen track's pan, left to right in 41 steps. The message band says it (PAN L 50, PAN C). Tracks start spread out: 1 in the middle, 2 half right, 3 and 4 a quarter left and right, 5 and 6 near the middle.
USB MIDI innotes play the chosen track, as the keys do.
MASTERthe level.

Generative paths

Each track has a path that leans what HOME draws, on every engine. A path changes nothing already playing: it shapes the next sounds drawn on that track. The path's key is lit while that track is chosen.

PathKeyLeans towards
AMBIENT1st black keysounds for ambient, dark ambient above all: ethereal, melodic, often melancholic. FM draws drones, beating spectra (SPECTRE), the depths (ABYSS), bells, voices (CHOIR), bowed, hollow, blooming and tidal tones, never BRUIT, IMPACT, FRICTION, SHARDS or STATIC — and plucks and mallets, never WARP, GLITCH or RUBBER; then softer attacks (a pluck or a mallet may keep its strike), long tails, darker modulators, slow LFOs, no sirens, narrower glides, often an octave down. ANIMA draws mostly HAZE, GOLDEN, VOYAGE, TIDE, CHOIR, BOWL, FOG and DRIFT, never GRIT, SHARDS, MACHINE, BITS or HOWL, with a darker tone, more space, a slower hand, long releases, no crusher. CALIGULA draws SPORE, VEIL and LITANY most, UNDERTOW, CARRION, MOTH, sometimes RUST; tuned on root, fifths, octaves, depths and unisons; slow swells, softer edges, fewer bursts and surges, a slower hand. RUSSOLO draws CHORD most, then DUST, CRACKLE, BLIPS, WALK and WANDER, never the logic kinds (NOR, XOR, RING, CASCADE, CLANG), JUMP, BEND or QUAD; clean (9–10 bits), slow attacks, long releases, calmer chance, no major chords
EXPERIMENTAL2nd black keysounds for electroacoustic and acousmatic music: edgier, gnarlier. FM draws bruits, frictions, shards, static, impacts, iterations, warps, glitches and rubber, brighter, bent more often (sometimes twice), never SPECTRE, CHOIR, BOWED or TIDE. ANIMA draws mostly GRIT, SWARM, SHARDS, MACHINE, BITS and HOWL, never HAZE, TIDE, CHOIR, FOG or DRIFT, and makes them wild: the sliders near their tops (FM, grain, texture, density, a quick hand), the resonance often screaming, and on most designs a crushed sample rate, folding drive, a band of noise and scattered grains, all dragged about by the hand, often a fast tremolo tearing it apart, the comb ringing hard. CALIGULA draws WIRE, THORN, HIVE and RUST most, never VEIL or LITANY; semitone clusters and tritones; sharper, more driven, more bursts and surges, a quicker hand. RUSSOLO draws NOR, XOR, CLANG, BEND and QUAD most, never WALK or CHORD; crushed to 4–9 bits, often sample-held, abrupt attacks and short releases, chance driving it hard
OPENneither litevery family, kind and species alike, as before the paths. Every track starts here

Sessions keep each track's path, and the path each of its sounds was drawn on.

Macros

Press EDIT (the black key just left of SHIFT; lit while on) and the four knobs across the top stop being the filter, the granulator, the crush and the send: they become four macros that reshape the chosen track's sound, while it plays, under a held note. Every macro answers early in the turn (a quarter of the way, half the change). Each is turned from the middle, which is the sound as HOME drew it; either way transforms it. While a knob turns, the whole screen is its dial, with the macro's name for this sound and how far it is turned (+40 %, -25 %, AS DRAWN). Press EDIT again to give the knobs back.

The macros are chosen for each engine, and for some by the kind of sound:

KNOB 1KNOB 2KNOB 3KNOB 4
FMBRIGHTNESS: the modulation index about 27 dB either way (down: towards pure sines; up: the feedback too), the carriers tilted (the higher partials up)DETUNE: the carriers pulled apart ±40 cents and the modulators ±25 cents off them — beating, chorus, the partials off their places — or INHARMONIC for metallic and noisy families (every partial off its ratio: clangour)SATURATION: feedback and saturation turning up; a low-pass, smoother, turning downMOTION: the LFO's depths; turning up, a tremolo, quicker and deeper
ANIMATONE: every filter four octaves up or down (sharper when up), the FM brighter or darkerwhat the kind is about, from nothing to far more: GRAINS, NOISE, FM (the index), FORMANT (sharper when up) or DRIVE (folded hard; turned down, a pure tone: the second voice, FM, noise and grains drawn out)RESONATOR: much wetter and ringing longer (brought in if the sound had none), or dryMOTION: the hand four times quicker, a tremolo pulsing — or nearly still, no tremolo
CALIGULAWAVEFORM: triangles to squaresMOD DEPTH: how deeply the pairs modulate each otherFEEDBACK (total feedback and drive) — or DELAY for SPORE, VEIL, LITANY and MOTHTOUCHES: how busy the hand is, its touches and bursts — or GATE RATE (the gates' speed) for HIVE, MOTH and WIRE
DRUIDSTRUCTURE: on a string, its dispersion (below a quarter, a buzzing bridge; above, the partials stretched, then noise in the period); on sympathetic strings, the intervals they are tuned to; on a body, how its partials are spaced, from squeezed through harmonic to bell-likeBRIGHTNESS: the exciter's low-pass and the string's or body's high-frequency lossDAMPING: how long it rings, from ~70 ms to ~18 s to -60 dB, and above 0.95 on without decayPOSITION: where it is plucked or struck and where it is picked up — which partials sound
BAYAREASHAPE: the oscillator from sine through triangle and square to sawFOLDS: the wavefolder's driveFM: both modulators' depthDECAY: the gate's decay, or the sustain's release, from an eighth to eight times the sound's own
RUSSOLOthe kind's first parameter (RATE, TONE, WIDTH, HISS, RATIO, SPREAD, DENSITY, SILENCE, WINDOW, STEP or DEPTH)the kind's second parameter (CHANCE, DENSITY, WANDER, DRIFT, SUB, CLOCK, CHANGE, JUMPS or RATE)CRUSH: fewer bits and longer sample holds, or cleanerRANDOMNESS: how much chance drives it; above the middle, stutters too

Each track keeps the macros of each of its six sounds. HOME draws a new sound as it comes (its macros in the middle). Sessions and presets keep the macros with the sound.

Envelope

The 3rd black key from the right opens the ENVELOPE page (the key is lit while it is up; pressed again, or a track button, closes it). It shows the amplitude envelope of the chosen track's sound as attack, decay, sustain and release, drawn and with their values. As HOME drew the sound, the page reads its own envelope and says AS DRAWN (in grey): for FM, the envelope of the loudest carrier; for CALIGULA, the average of its pairs' attacks and releases; CALIGULA and RUSSOLO have no decay or sustain stage (shown as 5 ms and 100 %).

While the page is up, the four knobs across the top set ATTACK (KNOB 1, 1 ms – 10 s), DECAY (KNOB 2, 5 ms – 10 s), SUSTAIN (KNOB 3, 0–100 %) and RELEASE (KNOB 4, 5 ms – 20 s), on logarithmic scales. The first turn starts from the values shown and replaces the sound's own amplitude envelope with this one: the attack is linear, the decay and release are exponential, the release ending 60 dB down. FM's carrier envelopes and ANIMA's envelope are then held at full; CALIGULA and RUSSOLO are kept playing through the release and then let go. The change applies from the next note; once the track's envelope is in use, turning the knobs also changes the notes that are sounding.

SHIFT + the key, HOME (a new sound) or loading a preset gives the sound's own envelope back. Each track keeps an envelope for each of its six engines. Sessions store them, copying a track copies them, presets do not.

BALLSY

SHIFT + EDIT turns on BALLSY, a physics sequencer of bouncing balls, for the chosen track and shows its page; EDIT blinks while it runs, and SHIFT + EDIT again turns it off. Each track has its own, and they run at the same time. Holding EDIT (0.6 s) while the chosen track's balls run puts their page down or up: with the page down the balls keep playing and the knobs, the screen and the other pages work as usual; a track button or another page also puts it down. A short press of EDIT still turns EDIT on or off.

One to eight balls move in a box on the screen. Each time a ball hits a wall, it plays a note on the track, as a key would: in the scale, with the loops' transposition and chord mode, and recorded by the looper when REC is on. Each note's length (50 ms to 1.5 s) and level (from −10 dB to full) are drawn at random; the level applies to FM, ANIMA and DRUID (CALIGULA and RUSSOLO play at their own level), and notes the looper records play back at full level. Each bounce changes the ball's angle at random by up to 12°, kept between 15° and 75° from the walls, so the paths change and every wall is reached. Each wall holds the notes of the scale, one segment per step, and the segment that is hit lights up. The pitch rises clockwise all the way round, one octave per wall:

WallOctave (at the start)Direction of rising pitch
bottom−1 (the octave below the keyboard's)right to left
left0 (the keyboard's)upwards
top+1left to right
right+2downwards

While their page is up, the four knobs control them:

Knob
KNOB 1the number of balls, 1–8; new ones start from the middle in a random direction
KNOB 2speed, 0–100 (from 0.08 to 2.4 box widths per second)
KNOB 3the octaves of the four walls, moved together by one octave per click, from −3…0 to +2…+5
KNOB 4instability, 0–100 (0 at the start): each ball gets its own wind, two values that wander at random (a new aim about twice a second, followed over ~0.3 s). One scales its speed, up to 8× faster or slower at 100, so a ball can nearly stop and then rush on; the other turns it, up to half a turn per second. Occasional gusts change its direction by up to 60°. At 0 the pace is steady and the paths straight

The screen shows the box, the walls' segments in the track's colour and the balls; the line above shows the number of balls, or the value just turned. Sessions store each track's ball settings and whether they are on; copying a track copies them.

Latched keys

Hold one or more white keys and press SHIFT (the rightmost black key): they latch, sounding on after you let go, and they stay lit. A key pressed while SHIFT is already held plays as usual (unless it is lit). Latches belong to the track they were made on: the keys are lit while that track is chosen, and on another track the same keys play as usual, so a drone can be left on one track while you play another. Pressing a latched key without SHIFT does nothing (it sounds already); SHIFT and the lit key lets go of it, and its note ends as a lifted key's would. Loading a session lets go of every latch. Latched notes hold voices of the shared pool: with all twelve busy, a new note can take one, even a latched one's.

Chords

With chord mode on for a track (the 3rd black key held 0.6 s; CHO at the top left of the screen, the form's abbreviation under it in grey: TRI, IN1, IN2, SU2, SU4, OPN, 4TH), each white key plays three notes: its own note and two more of the same scale, so every chord stays in the scale and its quality (major, minor, diminished) is the scale's at that degree. Pressing the 3rd black key steps through the forms (in steps of the scale from the key's note):

FormSteps
TRIAD0, 2, 4root, third, fifth (the start)
INV 12, 4, 7first inversion: the third at the bottom, the root an octave up
INV 2−3, 0, 2second inversion: the fifth below the root
SUS20, 1, 4the third replaced by the second
SUS40, 3, 4the third replaced by the fourth
OPEN0, 4, 9root, fifth, and the third an octave up
FOURTHS0, 3, 6stacked fourths

One chord sounds at a time on a track: a new key lets the one before go. Chords follow the loops' moves along the scale like single notes, latch with SHIFT (all three notes), are recorded by the loopers as three notes, and are kept in sessions (chord mode, its form, the chords latched); copying a track copies its chord mode.

Direction and speed

The 4th to 8th black keys set how the chosen track's loops play, all its overdubs together, each within its own length:

KeySetting
4th black keyREVERSE: the loops play backwards — each note starts where it ended and ends where it started
5th black keyPENDULUM: forwards to the end of each loop, backwards to its start, and so on
6th black keyRANDOM: the loops play forwards, but each time the next note is due (and at the loop's end) they jump to a note of the loop drawn at random and go on from there — each note keeps its length and the time to the note that followed it when recorded; notes struck together stay together; the notes sounding are let go at each jump
7th black keyHALF SPEED: the loops take twice as long (the pitch does not change)
8th black keyDOUBLE SPEED: the loops take half as long

REVERSE, PENDULUM and RANDOM exclude each other, as do HALF and DOUBLE; pressing the lit key again returns to forwards or to normal speed. Direction and speed combine (backwards at half speed, pendulum at double, and so on). Changing the direction while a loop plays continues from where it is: a note sounding at that moment carries on and ends where its start was. An overdub recorded at half or double speed, or while the loops play backwards, is stored so that it plays back as it was played. Sessions keep the settings; copying a track copies them; emptying a track's loops (REC held) returns them to forwards and normal speed.

Copying a track

Hold a track's button until the screen flashes COPIED / TRACK n: the track is on the clipboard, and its button blinks. Choose another track and hold its button until PASTED / TRACK n: it now has the copied track's tone and loops. The clipboard is then empty: the next hold copies again. Holding the copied track's own button again copies it again (as it is now), pasting nothing.

What is copied: the tone — the engine, the sounds of all six engines with their macros and envelopes, the filter, the granulator, the crush, the reverb send, the octave and the generative path — and all the loops, every overdub, those taken out still out, playing or stopped as they were (pasted, they start from their beginnings). The copy is taken when you hold the button: what the track does afterwards is not pasted. The track pasted onto keeps its level and pan (its place in the mix); whatever it had before is replaced, and its latched notes are let go.

The loopers

Every track has its own looper of up to ten loops, and they are all free: no tempo, no grid, no quantising — not even between a track's own loops. Each overdub is a loop of its own, as long as you made it (from its first note to REC), going round in its own length over the others, so they drift in and out of phase. Each plays back exactly what was played, to 0.73 ms. A note still held when REC closes the loop is tied over its end: it sounds on unbroken as the loop goes round, so a drone stays one long note rather than being struck again each time. The keys go on playing the track over its loops, and the loops' notes and the keys' never cut each other's notes off — but all of them share the pool's twelve voices with the other tracks, so many loops and tracks at once take voices from each other. A track's loops hold about 500 notes between them; nothing is lost when the FM-1 is switched off if the session is saved.

Bringing loops in and out. Hold PLAY (it does not start or stop anything held): the chosen track's loops appear on the white keys, the first loop — the foundation — on the leftmost, each overdub on the next, up to ten, lit while they play; the screen shows them too (in the track's colour: in; a grey frame: out). Press a key to take its loop out — its notes stop, the others go on — or to bring it back in: it comes in at once, from its start. With the loops stopped it chooses which will play: take out all but one, let go of PLAY, press PLAY, and only that one starts; then bring the others in, one by one, as the piece unfolds. Every loop is in when recorded. Sessions keep which loops are out.

Moving the loops along the scale. Hold SHIFT and press OCT+ or OCT−: every loop of every track moves one step of the chosen scale up or down — from C to D in C major, from C to D♯ in C minor pentatonic — so each loop keeps its shape within the scale. The notes sounding move at once; the screen shows how far the loops are moved (TRANSP +2, TRANSP -1, TRANSP 0), up to two octaves of the scale either way. Choosing another scale or root while they are moved walks the new one. A note outside the scale keeps its distance from the scale note below it. The white keys move with them: on a track, they play the scale moved as far as that track's loops are (all the loops' move and its own), so what you add fits what is there — and an overdub recorded while the loops are moved plays back as you played it, the others staying where they are. (USB MIDI notes are not moved.) Sessions keep how far the loops are moved.

One track's loops along the scale. Hold SHIFT, hold a track's button, and press OCT+ or OCT−: only that track's loops move (every overdub with them), a step of the scale at a time; the screen says TRANSP T3 +2. It adds to the move of all the loops, and that track's white keys and latched notes (and chords) move with it; SHIFT + OCT alone moves every track's latched notes with all the loops. The lit latched keys move along the keyboard by as many white keys, in the same direction (a latch that would leave the keyboard stays on its key, its note still moved). Holding the track's button with SHIFT down never copies it. Emptying a track's loops (REC held) takes its own move away; copying a track takes it along; sessions keep it.

The screen

From top to bottom: the track number (very large, in the track's colour), its engine (FM or ANIMA, in white), the family of its sound (in the track's colour). When something changes (NEW, OCT +1, LOOP), a black-on-white message replaces the family for a moment. While the chosen track's looper is armed the band below the engine flashes ARMED in red; while it records it shows REC, white on red. A message too long for the band at its usual size (EXPERIMENTAL) is drawn a size smaller. Under it, across the screen, the track's level meter: a bar filling from the left with the track's colour as it sounds (-48 to +6 dB), and a white mark at the level the SELECT knob sets (red at the left when the track is off). At the very bottom, the track's pan: a block in its colour on a track from left to right, with a tick at the middle.

KNOB 1 to 4 (filter, granulator, crush, reverb send) each show, while they turn and for a second after, the same full-screen dial: the knob's name and the track, an arc from 7 to 5 o'clock lit in the track's colour, a white pointer, and in large type what it does.

The REVERB page shows the title and its four values in rows, each with a bar; the row you just turned is drawn black on white for a moment.

Scales

One scale and root for the whole keyboard (and saved with the session); C major at the start. The root sits on the first white key, in the octave from C3 to B3 (each track's OCT moves it); the scale climbs from there across the 16 white keys, so a pentatonic scale spans more than three octaves.

ScaleSteps
MAJOR0 2 4 5 7 9 11
MINOR NATURAL0 2 3 5 7 8 10
MINOR HARMONIC0 2 3 5 7 8 11
MINOR MELODIC0 2 3 5 7 9 11
DORIAN0 2 3 5 7 9 10
MINOR PENTA0 3 5 7 10
WHOLE TONE0 2 4 6 8 10
ENIGMATIC0 1 4 6 8 10 11
JAPANESE IN0 1 5 7 8 — the in (miyako-bushi) scale of the koto and shakuhachi, known for its sorrow

USB MIDI notes are not quantised.

Presets

Each engine has 64 presets, P1 to P64, for the sounds you want to keep and bring back on any track. Hold SHIFT and press SAVE: the PRESETS page of the chosen track's engine opens, four slots a page. PRESETS turns through them; a slot holding a sound shows its number in red and the sound's name, an empty one EMPTY in grey.

  • SAVE held saves the track's sound into the slot chosen. Over a sound already there it asks OVERWRITE? first, on NO until PRESETS turns it to YES; SAVE answers.
  • SAVE loads the slot chosen into the track (which crossfades to it, as to a new sound) and goes back to playing.

A preset keeps what draws the sound again, exactly — its seed, its path and the generation of the generators that drew it — and its level: all 256 take one sector of flash, beside the sessions. Saving erases flash, which silences the audio for a moment, as a session save does.

Sessions

The FM-1 always starts with no session loaded. There are 64 slots, numbered 1–64.

A session stores in full the sound of the engine each track is on, and the other three as the seed that made them and their level (the same sounds, drawn again at once), so a session usually takes one 4 KB sector of flash. A session is the whole machine: every track's engine and its six sounds, its path, octave, level, pan, reverb send, filter, granulator (and the character it was drawn with), crush, distortion, envelopes, latched notes and loops (playing or stopped, each overdub in or out); the scale and root, the reverb, and the track chosen. They are kept in the FM-1's flash, in its user data area (saving overwrites any projects, presets or samples another firmware left there): dozens of typical sessions, at least ten even with six full loops. A session also keeps the seeds its sounds were made from, with the path and the generation of the generators that drew them: every generation is kept exactly as it was (a test checks thousands of sounds of each), so sessions and presets saved under an older Tonitor load with the same sounds after an update that brings new generators. Erasing flash silences the audio for a moment: a save uses blank flash when there is some, and the FM-1 blanks free flash by itself while nothing sounds.

The granulator

Each track keeps the last half second of its own sound (at 22 kHz, 8-bit mu-law: a little grit is part of it) and plays grains out of it, after its filter. Each track's granulator has a character of its own, drawn at random when the FM-1 starts and every time a session is loaded: the intervals its grains are pitched to, how often they reverse, stutter, drop out or freeze, the shape of its scattered grains, how far its feedback and darkening go, how it drifts. The knob's position is saved with the session; the character is drawn anew. When the track's notes end, its grains ring on for about two seconds.

The distortion

Each track has a distortion, set with SHIFT + KNOB 3 (0–100; 0 is off). It comes after the track's filter, granulator, crush and limiter, and before its level, pan and sends, so the delay and the reverb receive the distorted sound.

  • Two gain stages in series: the first symmetric (odd harmonics), the second asymmetric (even harmonics). The amount sets the drive into the first stage (×0.5 to ×32, up to +36 dB) and the second stage's gain and bias.
  • A bias in proportion to the input's own level is added before the first stage, so the clipped wave stays asymmetric and keeps its even harmonics at any drive. At low amounts the second harmonic dominates; higher amounts add more harmonics (on a sine, up to 14 of the first 15 above −60 dB).
  • The highs are raised 6 dB before the stages and lowered 6 dB after, so the mids and highs distort more than the bass. The stages run at twice the sample rate to reduce aliasing. A low-pass after them goes from 16 kHz down to 6.5 kHz as the amount goes up.
  • The output level is matched to the dry signal's RMS level (measured over about 0.2 s), so turning the amount up changes the drive and the harmonics, not the loudness.

Stored in sessions and copied with the track.

The delay

A master delay, mono, placed before the reverb: each track's delay send (SHIFT + KNOB 4) feeds it, its echoes go to both sides of the master, and half of their level also goes into the reverb, so the echoes are reverberated. Its line holds 2 seconds at 22.05 kHz in 8 bits (μ-law, as the granulator's), so the repeats are slightly dark and grainy.

Parameter
TIME20 ms to 2 s, on a logarithmic scale (shown in ms). Turning it glides the delay over about 0.1 s, so the repeats bend in pitch rather than click
FEEDBACKhow much of each repeat comes back: 0 (one repeat) to 0.95
DAMPa low-pass in the feedback path: each repeat darker than the one before
MIXthe level of the echoes

The delay's parameters and every track's send are kept in sessions; copying a track copies its send.

The reverb

A plate after Jon Dattorro (1997): predelay, input diffusion, and a figure-of-eight tank whose two allpasses sweep slowly out of step, so the tail stays in motion and never rings. Each track sends to it after its level; the reverb's return is added to the mix before the master.

at the start
SIZEthe room: every delay 0.5–1.25 times Dattorro's (turning it bends the tail, gently)70
DECAYthe time to fall 60 dB, 0.4 s to about 25 s, whatever the size65 (about 3.5 s)
DAMPhow fast the highs die in the tail40
MIXthe reverb's return level, ×0 to ×450 (×1)

Track colours: 1 yellow, 2 cyan, 3 pink, 4 green, 5 orange, 6 lilac.

The engines

FM — six operators, DX7 style

The classic six-operator FM (msfa, the core of Dexed: 32 algorithms, rate/level envelopes, ratio or fixed frequencies, feedback, LFO, pitch envelope). HOME draws a patch from one of twenty-two families of sound objects (since 0.22 with their operators on the ratios they were designed with — before, a slip in the generator put nearly every ratio near an even multiple and the patches two octaves above the key; sounds saved then come back as they were):

FamilyAfter
METALbells and gongs: many carriers on inharmonic ratios, the high partials dying first
DRONEspectral drones: near-harmonic pairs detuned to beat, an index wandering over minutes
BRUITnoises: feedback and high ratios scattered by a sample-and-hold LFO
IMPACTstruck bodies, the pitch falling, the modulators dying before the carriers
ITERATIFiterative objects: a sound pulsed by its own LFO, square or random
GLISSEglissandi: a pitch envelope travelling octaves, slowly
SPECTREa spectral arpeggio: rich tones a few cents apart whose beating lifts one harmonic after another
ABYSSsub-bass rumble folded by feedback, breathing slowly
FRICTIONcreaking: sub-audio fixed-frequency modulators and random pitch
CHOIRvowels: carriers on the harmonics nearest two formants, a late vibrato
BOWEDa bowed string: a saw from feedback, the bow's pressure rising with the swell
HOLLOWodd harmonics only: a dark pipe
BLOOMa tone that opens over seconds and half closes again
TIDEthree stacks crossfading, one fading as the next swells, under a slow tide of level
SHARDSa tone broken by random steps of pitch and chopped by a square
STATICring-modulated bands from modulators nailed to audio frequencies
WINDbreath and gusts over a soft drone
PLUCKplucked strings, bright or dark: the modulators die at once (the attack's brightness), the carriers die away, higher strings quicker
MALLETstruck bars — marimba, vibraphone, kalimba: a high modulator's knock, gone at once, the bar ringing on
WARPanything: ratios anywhere, partials nailed to frequencies, the pitch bent about by its envelope
GLITCHa quick sample-and-hold stepping the pitch and the level, envelopes chopped short
RUBBERlow ratios and the pitch bouncing in at every note: up past it, back under, onto it

Each patch is then shaped with care: modulators on high ratios turned down (their sidebands alias and scream), the brightness scaled down the keyboard so high notes are not shrill nor low ones muddy, rate scaling on the carriers. HOME draws several patches, measures each, and keeps one whose brightness suits the track's path (darker on AMBIENT, brighter on EXPERIMENTAL) and that is not of the family the track had.

Since 0.29 (generation 3) a patch may also be made plucked whatever its family, have a modulator moved to another ratio, or an operator detuned against the rest; the last five families are drawn only from then. About half the patches are then bent once more, gently (an operator detuned to beat, an envelope turned over to grow as it holds, the LFO waiting and then moving the timbre, an octave down, more feedback, a modulator's ratio moved to a neighbour, a partial nailed to a frequency). Every patch is rendered offline as it is made and given the gain that brings it to one loudness.

ANIMA — a lo-fi synthesizer played by a simulated hand

ANIMA is the lo-fi engine: each voice runs at half the sample rate (22.05 kHz, so nothing above 11 kHz), its samples drawn out to the full rate by straight lines between them. Its pitches, rates and filters are scaled to sound where they would at the full rate; what goes is the top octave of air — and half of the chip's time, so more voices sound at once.

A fixed-point port of the anima opcode from Vascular, rebuilt for the FM-1. While a key is held, a simulated finger rests on a virtual surface and drags one figure after another — orbits, figures of eight, scribbles, slow glides, now and then a flick — pressing in slow swells, and now and then lifting to land elsewhere. A ghost finger comes and goes on an irregular clock. Where the finger is, how hard it presses, how fast it moves and how long it has been down move the timbre, never the pitch.

The voice: two wavetable oscillators (24 band-limited single cycles), an FM pair, a stack of copies, a grain cloud, a filtered noise, a resonant filter, a wavetable tremolo; then the hand's chain: a downsampler, a waveshaper, a phaser, a second filter and a comb resonator tuned to the note. Each new sound is a design: which of these are in, on which waveforms, and for every parameter which gesture moves it, over what range, along what curve, plus a mod matrix of three to seven routes and Anima's eight sliders, drawn — often far from their middle. Twenty-two kinds: HAZE, VOYAGE, GLASS, BELLS, GOLDEN (Anima's own) and BREATH, GRIT, SWARM, TIDE (waves of noise over a low drone), CHOIR (vowels, a formant the hand moves), SHARDS (glass grains scattered and crushed), BOWL (a beating inharmonic hum in a ringing comb), DUST (sparse crackle over a dark drone), MACHINE (a pulsing, folded mechanism), and since 0.29 PLUCK (a plucked string: a burst through the comb tuned to the note, dying away), REED (nasal, through a formant the hand moves, a breath in it), FOG (a stack under fog, a slow phaser drifting through it), ORGAN (drawbars, a rotary tremolo, a little drive), BITS (pulses in few bits: the rate crushed and dragged about, folded), DRIFT (two saws drifting against each other, a chorus the hand moves), MURMUR (a dark cloud of noisy grains) and HOWL (noise through a resonance so sharp it whistles, swept by the hand). Every kind draws wider since 0.29 (generation 3): any of the 24 waveforms, wider intervals and ratios, a detuning, now and then a plucked envelope or a slow swell, another way for the hand to move, a pulsing tremolo, a crushed rate or a sharp resonance. The filter follows the keyboard, so low notes are not muffled nor high ones shrill; the second oscillator's interval suits the path (consonant on AMBIENT, anything on EXPERIMENTAL); and an AMBIENT sound nearly always has a resonant space to ring in.

In Vascular a design plays up to six fingers, each a voice; here a track has one voice, so the hand has one finger on the sound.

CALIGULA — an organism

The third engine, after the architecture of SOMA's LYRA-8 as Mike Moreno's LIRA-8 emulates it (BSD licence), rebuilt for the FM-1 and bent towards dark, restless textures. Eight oscillators in four pairs on two sides; each a triangle that its pair's SHARP pushes towards a square; each with a sensor and an envelope, slow (a long swell, a longer fall) or fast; each pair frequency-modulated at audio rate by its partner, the other pair of its side, a pair of the other side or the total feedback (the whole organism, saturated, fed back in). A hyper LFO of two LFOs (alone, AND, OR, XOR) opens and closes the modulation and gates chosen pairs into irregular rhythms; a short modulated delay (two lines, ~35 ms) choruses, flanges or warps it; a drive.

A CALIGULA track is played like the others: the white keys play the scale's notes, and it is silent until a key is down. A key wakes the organism at that note; a second key on top moves the whole organism to the new note at once (a snap, not a glide), and letting go of it goes back to the key still held; letting go of the last key lifts the hand and the organism rings out. It is rooted: tuned around the note played, in intervals of it (octaves, fifths, unisons and semitone clusters that beat, tritones, the depths). The hyper LFO moves timbre, never pitch: no sirens.

Nobody touches the eight plates: a simulated hand does, while a key is held. Each species has its own hand: how often it touches, how long a finger stays, how many fingers at most, its favourite plates, quick taps against long holds. The first finger stays down until the key is let go, so the sound never drops out under a held key. Around the hand the organism has a life of its own: the modulation depths and the sharpness wander, oscillators fire in bursts at irregular times, and now and then the feedback and the drive surge for a moment. A pair's envelope may be slow: a swell of seconds, a release of up to nine seconds after the key is let go.

The hand often has a phrase: two to four plates it keeps coming back to, varied now and then, often on a pulse of its own (long, short, short, longer) — so it plays like someone rather than like chance. A pair the hyper LFO's gates never close stays under it all. HOME draws a new organism from ten species, tuned on one of ten sets of intervals (pillars of octaves and fifths, semitone clusters, the depths, the harmonics, unisons, tritones, fourths, a minor seventh, open fifths, a quarter-tone cluster):

Species
SPOREslow swells, held drones, breathing; low
THORNsharp, deep FM, driven, bursting often
HIVEthe hyper LFO quick and gating: irregular rhythms, bursts
CARRIONthe depths, heavy total feedback, the delay warped by the voices, surges
VEILmostly triangles, light modulation: the calmest
RUSTdriven, cross-modulated, surging, sometimes rhythmic
LITANYa slow choir: unisons and octaves beating, nothing sharp, a hand that stays
UNDERTOWdeep: heavy feedback and a warped delay pulling it under, slow surges
WIREhigh and sharp, clusters and quarter tones, a quick hand tapping, bursts
MOTHsoft triangles fluttering through the gates, on a pulse

RUSSOLO — noise, logic and broken buffers

The fourth engine re-makes the techniques of Robert Heel's Noisferatu (GPL-3.0) in fixed point, for the keys. It runs at a third of the sample rate (about 14.7 kHz) in 10-bit values, each held until the next — the grit of a small DAC — then reduces its bits and holds its samples further as the sound says.

A RUSSOLO track is played like the others and is silent until a key is down: the key opens an envelope and sets the pitch (the oscillators' frequency, the speed a buffer is read at, the rate noise is sampled at); a second key on top moves it there at once; letting go of the last key lets it fade. Like CALIGULA it is one organism a track, outside the pool of voices. HOME draws one of seventeen kinds:

Kind
HOLDsample-and-hold noise, its rate from the key
DUSTrandom clicks through a low-pass that follows the key
GATESnoise opened and closed by two triangles, one wandering off the other
CRACKLEsparse clicks ringing on short pitched decays, over hiss
NOR, XORtwo oscillators combined bit by bit
RINGtwo oscillators multiplied
CASCADEsquares modulating squares, a sub-octave below
CLANGtwo triangles at an inharmonic ratio, XOR'd; the ratio redrawn when two clocks meet
CHUNKSa generated buffer of noise, saw and silent chunks, read at the key's speed and rebuilt in parts
JUMPthe buffer read with jumps at random
WANDERa window wandering through the buffer
BENDan address bit of the buffer forced to 0 or 1, flipped or held; which and how change on a clock
QUADfour such bendings at once, each switched on and off by chance
BLIPSdecaying triangles fired by chance on the key's harmonics
WALKa random walk over a scale's steps from the key
CHORDtriangles on the key (minor, major, open fifths or suspended), slowly beating and swelling

Each kind has two parameters of its own, the first two macros; CRUSH and CHAOS are the other two. Its level is measured when it is drawn, and never raised so far that its loudest click could clip.

DRUID — strings and resonant bodies

The fifth engine is a fixed-point port of the resonators of Mutable Instruments Rings by Émilie Gillet (MIT licence). It plays from the shared pool of voices, like FM and ANIMA. Each kind is one of Rings' resonators and an exciter:

Resonator
Stringa Karplus-Strong string: a delay line read with Hermite interpolation, damped by a short FIR filter (brightness) and a state-variable low-pass, its decay set as a time to −60 dB. Dispersion (STRUCTURE) stretches the partials with an all-pass stage, adds noise to the period near the top, or below a quarter of the range bends the bridge so the string buzzes. The output is picked up at the position along the string
Sympathetic stringsa string and three more tuned to intervals of its note (octaves, fifths, a twelfth, chosen by STRUCTURE), driven only by the first string's sound; their pickup positions drift slowly
Modalup to 16 two-pole resonators at the partials of a bar or plate, stretched or squeezed by STRUCTURE; each partial's level depends on the position
Exciter
PluckRings' plucker: a burst of noise as long as the position's share of the period, through a comb filter and a low-pass
Strikea short pulse, longer and softer as the brightness goes down
Bownoise for as long as the key is held, swelling in and dying away when released
Dustrandom impacts for as long as the key is held
KindResonatorExciter
PLUCKstringpluck
BOWEDstringbow
STRUCKstring, stretched partialsstrike
SITARstring, buzzing bridgepluck
RATTLEstringdust
HARPsympathetic stringspluck
DRONEsympathetic stringsbow
BELLmodalstrike
BOWLmodalbow
PLATEmodaldust

AMBIENT favours BOWED, HARP, DRONE, BELL and BOWL, with long decays that carry on after the key is released; EXPERIMENTAL favours RATTLE and PLATE, with shorter decays, faster dust, extreme positions and a stronger damping when the key is released. Releasing a key damps the sound by an amount set per sound, from ringing on to stopping short. Each voice's delay lines are 16-bit and use the memory an ANIMA voice would use: a string reaches down to about 29 Hz, and sympathetic strings that would not fit their shorter lines are tuned an octave up.

BAYAREA — a West Coast voice

The sixth engine is a fixed-point port of the bayarea opcode of Vascular, contributed by its author. It plays from the shared pool of voices, like FM, ANIMA and DRUID. Each voice has:

  • an oscillator that morphs from sine through triangle and square to saw (SHAPE), its frequency modulated linearly, through zero, by two sines at ratios of it (0.66 and 3.3 by default, other ratios on some sounds), each ratio wandering slightly and slowly;
  • a wavefolder (FOLDS), reflecting the wave back into range;
  • a 12 kHz smoothing low-pass and a trace of noise;
  • either a low-pass gate, where a resonant low-pass and an amplifier are struck together by one-shot envelopes (an attack of 2–3 ms and a decay), or a sustaining envelope over two resonant low-passes (an attack while the key is held, a release when it is let go). The filters sweep from 300 Hz to the sound's peak frequency, higher for louder notes;
  • a saturating output stage (tanh, then a soft clip) with its own drive;
  • a bank of three resonators (508, 270 and 1153 Hz, ringing for 1–1.4 s), mixed in by the sound's amount;
  • an LFO (triangle, ramp, square or random steps) that moves the shape, the folds, the two FM depths, the attack, the peak, the decay and the resonator mix, by amounts drawn with the sound.

Changed from the opcode: the square and saw are band-limited with polyBLEP instead of being summed from 44 partials (too costly for this chip), and the opcode's reverb is replaced by the track's sends to the master delay and reverb, keeping only its resonator bank.

KindEnvelope
BONGOgatelow peak, short decay, little folding
PLUCKgatebrighter, square to saw, short to medium decay
CHIMEgatethe upper modulator deep, long decay, resonators
FOLDEDgateheavy folding
SWELLsustainslow attack (0.3–3 s), long release
DRONEsustainslower attack (0.5–4 s), the lower modulator deep, long release

AMBIENT favours BONGO, CHIME, SWELL and DRONE; EXPERIMENTAL favours PLUCK and FOLDED, with more drive and folding and other FM ratios more often.
